title: Selectors: type, class, id and groups
summary: Pick exactly the elements you want to style using type, class, id and grouped selectors.

quiz.explain: A class selector starts with a dot: `.note`. A hash `#` is for ids.
An id selector starts with `#`. Each id should appear only once in a page.

quiz.q: What does `h1, h2 { color: navy; }` do?
options: Styles only h2 elements inside an h1
Styles every h1 and every h2
Styles an element that is both h1 and h2
quiz.explain: A comma groups selectors. Both get the same declarations, which saves you from writing the rule twice.

quiz.q: The paragraph has `class="intro"`. Click the line whose selector will not match it.
quiz.explain: Without a dot, `intro` looks for an element named `<intro>`. Write `.intro`.

exercise.task:
Write CSS for the page. Work in `index.html`.

- Make every `h1` and `h2` dark blue using one grouped rule (`navy`).
- Make elements with class `note` have an orange `color`.
- Make the element with id `warning` red and bold (`font-weight: bold`).
hints: Type selectors are tag names, class selectors start with a dot, id selectors start with a hash.
Group two selectors with a comma: `h1, h2 { ... }`. The class rule is `.note { ... }` and the id rule is `#warning { ... }`.

checks.name: Every h2 is navy
checks.hint: Group h1 and h2 in the same rule.

checks.name: Elements with class note are orange
checks.hint: Use .note { color: orange; } with a leading dot.

checks.name: The #warning element is bold
checks.hint: Add font-weight: bold; to the #warning rule.

checks.name: Plain paragraphs are not orange
checks.hint: Only the .note paragraphs should be orange. Do not style the p type selector.
